learningPoints.title: Mass and weight: meanings and the distinction between them
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state what mass is, state what weight is, and explain why they are distinct quantities rather than two names for the same thing.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Mass is a measure of how much matter a body contains (an inertial property), measured in kilograms. Weight is the force exerted on that body by gravity (or the force needed to support it against gravity), measured in newtons. Mass does not change with location; weight does, because it depends on the local gravitational field. Colloquial use of 'weight' as a synonym for mass is technically incorrect.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-NIST-MASS: mass definition, weight definition, mass-weight distinction
learningPoints.depthJustification: Mass, weight, and their distinction are combined into one learning point because they form a single inseparable teachable comparison at this level -- a learner is not meaningfully diagnosed as 'knowing mass' or 'knowing weight' in isolation from the other; the comparison IS the concept. Purely definitional: carries no cross-domain (mathematics) prerequisite of its own, since it has no calculation outcome (that is EFS-LP-02, the weight-force relationship and its calculations).
explicitExclusions: The weight-force formula F=mg itself and any calculation using it (see MM-LP-02)
Relativistic or inertial-vs-gravitational mass distinctions
applicationTypes: Explain why an astronaut's mass is unchanged on the Moon while their weight is much less than on Earth.
State whether a bathroom scale reading in kilograms is measuring mass or weight.

learningPoints.title: Weight force: F = mg and mass/weight calculations
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state the relationship F=mg between weight force, mass and gravitational field strength, and use it (including rearranged) to calculate a weight from a mass or a mass from a known weight.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The weight force on a body equals its mass multiplied by the gravitational field strength: F=mg (g is approximately 9.8 m/s^2 near the Earth's surface). This defines the weight force whenever a body is near a gravitational field -- it is not restricted to objects in free fall. The formula rearranges to m=F/g to find mass from a known weight force.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-MASS: w=mg
SRC-OPENSTAX-MASSWEIGHT: worked weight/mass calculations
learningPoints.depthJustification: The relationship (F=mg) and its use in calculation are combined into one learning point, since a learner who 'knows F=mg' and one who 'can calculate a weight or mass with it' are exhibiting the same skill applied to numbers -- separating them would be an artificial fragment (the same reasoning already applied to Ohm's law in the accepted Batch 02 inventory). F=mg is deliberately stated as an unconditional definition of the gravitational weight force, not restricted to free-fall, per the locked depth boundary for this batch. Weight is directly proportional to mass for a fixed g (hence FM-LP-10).
explicitExclusions: F=ma as an independent topic (this batch's weight-force relationship is F=mg specifically, the gravitational special case, not general Newtonian dynamics)
Variation of g with altitude/location as a calculated quantity
applicationTypes: Calculate the weight force of a 25 kg component.
Calculate the mass of an object given its weight force in newtons.

learningPoints.title: Levers: parts and basic operation
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to identify the fulcrum, effort and load on a lever and explain, in outline, how a lever works.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a fixed pivot point called the fulcrum. The effort is the force applied to the lever; the load (or resistance) is the force being overcome or moved.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-UIUC-LEVERS: lever definition and parts
SRC-UW-SIMPLEMACHINES: confirming
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from lever classes (MM-LP-04) and lever calculations (MM-LP-05) because identifying the parts of a lever, classifying a lever, and calculating with a lever are three separately-diagnosable skills -- a learner may correctly identify effort/load/fulcrum on a diagram while still being unable to classify the lever's class or calculate a balance, and vice versa.
explicitExclusions: Lever classification (see MM-LP-04)
Moment/balance calculations (see MM-LP-05)
applicationTypes: Label the fulcrum, effort and load on a diagram of a crowbar being used to lift a paving slab.

learningPoints.title: Lever classes
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to classify a lever as first, second or third class according to the relative positions of its fulcrum, effort and load.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Levers are classified strictly by the relative position of effort, load and fulcrum: first class (fulcrum between effort and load), second class (load between fulcrum and effort), third class (effort between fulcrum and load). A third-class lever has a mechanical disadvantage (effort exceeds load) but moves the load through a greater distance than the effort moves.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-UIUC-LEVERS: three lever classes
SRC-UW-SIMPLEMACHINES: confirming, with third-class mechanical-disadvantage note
learningPoints.depthJustification: The mastery outcome is the POSITIONAL classification rule itself, not memorising specific example objects (crowbar, wheelbarrow, tweezers) -- per the Product Architect's explicit instruction. Examples are used only as illustrations within applicationTypes, never as the assessed knowledge itself.
explicitExclusions: Memorising a fixed list of named example objects as the mastery outcome
Numerical mechanical-advantage calculation for each class (see MM-LP-05)
applicationTypes: Given a labelled diagram of a lever with the fulcrum, effort and load marked, state which class it belongs to.
Explain why a wheelbarrow is a second-class lever.

learningPoints.title: Lever calculations: effort, load and arm lengths
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to use the relationship Effort x Effort-Arm = Load x Load-Arm to calculate an unknown effort, load, or arm length for a lever in balance.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: At equilibrium, a lever balances when the effort force multiplied by its distance from the fulcrum (the effort arm) equals the load force multiplied by its distance from the fulcrum (the load arm): Effort x Effort-Arm = Load x Load-Arm. For a given rotation of the lever, the distance each point moves is proportional to its own distance from the fulcrum (its arm length): the effort and load therefore move through distances in the SAME ratio as their respective arm lengths -- the INVERSE of the force ratio (a point with a longer arm moves a proportionally greater distance but requires a proportionally smaller force to move it, and vice versa). Arm length and distance travelled are related but distinct quantities: arm length is fixed by the lever's geometry, while distance travelled also depends on how far the lever is rotated.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-COMFSM-LEVERTORQUE: Fe x de = Fr x dr
SRC-UW-SIMPLEMACHINES: moment balance, worked velocity-ratio example
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept as its own learning point, separate from MM-LP-03/MM-LP-04, per the Product Architect's explicit instruction that lever calculations are separately diagnosable from identifying parts or classifying a lever -- a learner may know what a lever is and its class without yet being able to calculate a balance. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the distance/arm-length relationship previously stated the ratio backwards (as the inverse of the arm ratio); it is now stated correctly as the SAME ratio as the arm lengths (the inverse of the force ratio), with arm length kept explicitly distinct from distance travelled by a point on the lever.
explicitExclusions: Torque/moment as a formal rotational-mechanics topic beyond the lever balance itself
Compound lever systems (multiple linked levers)
applicationTypes: Given an effort force and both arm lengths, calculate the maximum load a lever can balance.
Given a load, its arm length, and the effort arm length, calculate the effort force required.

learningPoints.title: Gears: what they do, driver and driven gears
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain what gears do, identify the driver (input) and driven (output) gear in a simple gear pair, and state the rotation direction of two directly-meshing external gears.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Gears transmit rotational motion and torque from one shaft to another shaft via their meshing teeth. The gear connected to the input (e.g. a motor) is the driver (input) gear; the gear connected to the output load is the driven (output) gear; any gears in between are idler gears. Two gears meshing directly with external teeth rotate in opposite directions.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-CUNY-GEARS: driver/driven/idler gears
SRC-PSU-GEARDIRECTION: general definition (transmits motion/torque between shafts, meshes via teeth) and opposite rotation direction
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from the gear-ratio/speed/torque calculation outcome (MM-LP-07) so a learner who can identify a driver/driven gear and rotation direction, but cannot yet calculate a ratio, is diagnosed correctly. Gears are never claimed to create or increase power anywhere in this learning point or its evidence, per the Product Architect's explicit instruction. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the general 'what a gear does' definition was previously attributed to a passage (SRC-CUNY-GEARS) that in fact supports only the driver/driven/idler definitions; it is now bound to an exact passage from the already-registered SRC-PSU-GEARDIRECTION source instead.
explicitExclusions: Internal (ring) gears, which do not follow the opposite-rotation rule
Gear-ratio speed/torque calculations (see MM-LP-07)
applicationTypes: Given a diagram of two meshing external gears with one driven by a motor, identify the driver and driven gear and state the driven gear's direction of rotation.

learningPoints.title: Gear ratio: speed and torque relationships
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate a gear ratio from the number of teeth on the driver and driven gears, use it to calculate the resulting output speed from a known input speed, and explain that, in the ideal (lossless) gear model, an increase in torque through a gear train corresponds to a proportional decrease in rotational speed, and vice versa.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The gear ratio (GR) is defined as GR = (teeth on the driven/output gear) / (teeth on the driver/input gear). Rotational speed scales by the INVERSE of the gear ratio: OutputSpeed = InputSpeed x (driver teeth/driven teeth) -- this speed relationship holds for any meshing gear pair, regardless of losses. In the IDEAL (lossless) gear model, torque at the output scales BY the gear ratio (OutputTorque = InputTorque x GR); since speed scales by the inverse of the same ratio, an arrangement that increases torque necessarily decreases rotational speed proportionally, and vice versa. Real gear trains lose some torque to friction between meshing teeth and in their bearings, so an actual output torque is somewhat less than this ideal value; the DIRECTION of the torque/speed trade-off still holds for real gear trains, but the exact equation is an ideal-model simplification, not an unconditional property of real, lossy gears.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-CUNY-GEARS: GR=output/input, OutputSpeed=InputSpeed x Input/Output, WheelTorque=MotorTorque x GR (ideal/lossless model), torque/speed trade-off
SRC-PSU-GEARDIRECTION: confirming the same GR=output/input convention
learningPoints.depthJustification: The speed calculation and the torque/speed trade-off are combined into one learning point because they are the same single gear-ratio relationship viewed from two angles (calculating a specific output speed, and explaining the general inverse trade-off with torque) -- both are derived from the identical GR=output/input definition in the same evidence, and splitting them would fragment one coherent outcome. The gear-ratio convention (numerator=output/driven, denominator=input/driver) is stated explicitly and used identically throughout, confirmed consistent across two independently-retrieved sources. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the torque relationship (OutputTorque=InputTorque x GR) is now explicitly framed as the ideal, lossless gear model rather than an unconditional property of real gear trains, which lose some torque to friction; this does not change the evidence status, since the source itself describes the ideal relationship and the qualifier is an honest scoping, not a retraction.
explicitExclusions: Compound gear trains with multiple idler-gear stages (only a simple two-gear pair is evidenced)
Gear efficiency/losses as a calculated quantity (see MM-LP-11, which covers real losses generally, only qualitatively)
applicationTypes: Calculate the gear ratio for a driver gear with 12 teeth and a driven gear with 36 teeth, and find the output speed for a given input speed.
Explain why a gear train that increases torque at the output must reduce the output's rotational speed.

learningPoints.title: Pulleys: purpose and basic operation
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain what a pulley is for and describe, at an appropriate level, how a fixed pulley and a system with movable pulleys each affect the force needed to lift a load.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A pulley is a wheel-and-rope mechanism used to lift objects. A single fixed pulley changes only the direction of the applied force (it does not reduce the force needed). Adding movable pulleys to the system can reduce the force needed to lift a given load.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-UWMADISON-PULLEY: fixed vs movable pulley operation
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from mechanical advantage (MM-LP-09) so basic pulley operation (what it is, fixed vs. movable) is diagnosed independently from the numerical mechanical-advantage rule.
explicitExclusions: Detailed lifting-equipment regulation or pulley-block inspection
Mechanical-advantage calculation (see MM-LP-09)
applicationTypes: Explain why a single fixed pulley at the top of a flagpole makes raising a flag easier even though it does not reduce the force needed.

learningPoints.title: Mechanical advantage
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state what mechanical advantage means for a machine in general, and calculate the ideal mechanical advantage of a pulley system by correctly counting the rope sections that support the load.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Mechanical advantage is the factor by which a machine multiplies an applied (effort) force to produce a larger output (load) force; for an ideal, frictionless machine this is the ideal mechanical advantage. For a pulley system specifically, the ideal mechanical advantage equals the number of rope sections that directly support the load (the weight end) -- not the total number of pulleys or the total rope length.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-SIMMAC: mechanical advantage as force-multiplying factor
SRC-UWMADISON-PULLEY: pulley MA = number of supporting rope sections
learningPoints.depthJustification: The general mechanical-advantage concept and its specific pulley-counting rule are combined because the counting rule is simply the pulley-specific instance of the same general concept; the rule for what counts as a 'supporting rope section' is bound exactly as the source defines it (the sections at the load end, not total rope length or pulley count), per the Product Architect's explicit caution. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: decimal-arithmetic, ratio-notation and substitution cross-domain prerequisites were removed, since the outcome's actual procedure is counting load-supporting rope sections, which requires none of those skills; attaching them was a defensive, not genuinely-required, dependency.
explicitExclusions: Actual (real, friction-reduced) mechanical advantage as distinct from ideal mechanical advantage (see MM-LP-11 for real losses generally)
applicationTypes: Given a diagram of a block-and-tackle pulley system, count the supporting rope sections and state the ideal mechanical advantage.

learningPoints.title: Ideal machines: the force-distance trade and the input/output power relationship
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain that an ideal machine trades a reduction in effort force for a proportional increase in the distance moved (and vice versa), that its work input equals its work output, and that -- for such an ideal machine with no internal energy storage, comparing input and output over the same time interval (i.e. in steady operation) -- input mechanical power equals output mechanical power; not that power is a generally conserved quantity in itself.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: For an ideal (frictionless) machine, Force_input x distance_input = Force_output x distance_output: a smaller effort force acting through a larger distance trades for a larger output force acting through a smaller distance, and this means the machine's work input equals its work output. Since power is the rate of doing work (P=W/t), comparing the input and the output over the SAME time interval, with no energy stored or released inside the machine between input and output, gives P_input=W_input/t=W_output/t=P_output for the ideal case -- a restricted consequence of the work equality and the definition of power, not an independent 'power conservation law', and not applicable to a machine that stores energy (e.g. a flywheel or spring) or when input and output are compared over different time intervals. An ideal machine can trade force for distance (or torque for speed) but can never output more work, energy, or power than is supplied to it.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-SIMMAC: Work_input=Work_output, force-distance trade
SRC-UWMADISON-PULLEY: pulley rope-length trade-off
SRC-UW-SIMPLEMACHINES: worked hydraulic force-distance example
Derived (SRC-HP-SIMMAC + SRC-PSU-POWER): explicitly-qualified input-power-equals-output-power relationship for an ideal, no-storage machine compared over the same time interval
learningPoints.depthJustification: The force-distance trade and the qualified power relationship are combined into one learning point because they are the same underlying principle viewed from two angles. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the power-equality statement is now bound only under its genuine conditions -- no internal energy storage, and input/output compared over the same time interval (steady operation) -- rather than as an unrestricted claim that 'power is conserved'; it is a transparent, explicitly-derived synthesis of the independently-verified ideal-machine work equality and the independently-verified P=W/t definition, not a claim made directly by either source alone. This is a purely conceptual/explanatory learning point (no numeric calculation is asked of the learner), so its cross-domain arithmetic prerequisites (previously attached defensively) have been removed. Kept separate from real losses (MM-LP-11), which covers the non-ideal case where this equality does not hold exactly.
explicitExclusions: Real (non-ideal) machines and friction losses (see MM-LP-11)
Hydraulic pressure-multiplication systems as their own Unit 202 topic (used only as confirming evidence of the general principle, not as taught content)
Any claim that power is a generally conserved quantity independent of this specific ideal, no-storage, same-interval case
Machines that store or release internal energy (e.g. flywheels, springs) as a context for this relationship
applicationTypes: Explain why a machine that reduces the effort force needed to lift a load must require the effort to move further.
Explain why, for an ideal machine operating steadily with no internal energy storage, the power delivered to the input must equal the power delivered at the output.

learningPoints.title: Real machines: friction and losses reduce useful output
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain that real machines are never perfectly efficient because friction and similar losses convert some input work or power into heat rather than useful output.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a real (non-ideal) machine, friction and similar loss mechanisms mean that not all of the input work or power reaches the useful output; the lost portion is converted into heat rather than delivered as useful mechanical output. This is why the useful output of a real machine is always less than its input.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-PSU-EFFICIENCY: friction losses converted to heat
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from the ideal-machine principle (MM-LP-10) because a learner may understand the ideal (energy-conserving) case perfectly while not yet grasping that real machines fall short of it -- these are independently diagnosable. Purely qualitative: no calculation formula is bound here (efficiency's own numerical calculation is MM-LP-17), so no cross-domain arithmetic prerequisite is attached.
explicitExclusions: Detailed friction-coefficient calculations
Quantifying the loss (that is efficiency, see MM-LP-17)
applicationTypes: Explain why a real pulley system requires a slightly greater effort force than the ideal mechanical-advantage calculation predicts.

learningPoints.title: Force
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that a force is a push or a pull, describe its possible effects (causing or changing motion, or causing deformation), and state its SI unit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A force is a push or a pull exerted on a body; it may produce motion, change existing motion, or cause the body to deform. The SI unit of force is the newton (N), defined as the force required to give a one-kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second squared.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-NIST-FORCE: force as push/pull, newton definition
learningPoints.depthJustification: A single, purely definitional/qualitative learning point at Unit 202 depth. Deliberately excludes F=ma as an independent topic and vector mechanics, per the Product Architect's locked exclusions.
explicitExclusions: F=ma as an independent Unit 202 topic
Vector addition/resolution of forces
Newton's three laws as a formal system
applicationTypes: Give two examples of forces acting in an everyday situation and state whether each is a push or a pull.

learningPoints.title: Work: concept and W = Fd
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain what work means in mechanics and use W=Fd to calculate the work done by a force acting along the direction of displacement.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Work is done when a force acts on an object and moves it through a distance in the direction of the force: W=Fd (work in joules = force in newtons x distance in metres, for a force acting along the direction of the displacement). One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre in the direction of the force.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-WORK: work definition and W=Fd
SRC-UW-SIMPLEMACHINES: confirming worked example
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definition and formula combined, as one concept (the same reasoning already applied to Ohm's law and F=mg in this and the accepted Batch 02 inventory). Deliberately scoped to the case where the force acts along the direction of displacement, per the locked depth boundary -- not generalised to an arbitrary force angle. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the formula-rearrangement prerequisite (FM-LP-16) was removed, since the evidenced worked examples (and this outcome) only ever calculate W from F and d -- no rearrangement to find F or d from the other two is evidenced.
explicitExclusions: Work done by a force at an angle to the displacement (the cos(theta) case)
Negative work / work done against a force as a separate formal topic (the specific case of work against gravity is covered in MM-LP-15)
applicationTypes: Calculate the work done pushing a trolley 8 m with a steady force of 15 N acting in the direction of travel.

learningPoints.title: Energy, kinetic energy and potential energy: concepts
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state what energy is, and explain the qualitative distinction between kinetic energy (energy of motion) and potential energy (stored energy due to position).
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Energy is the capacity of a system to do work, measured in joules. Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses because of its motion. Potential energy is energy associated with an object's position or configuration -- a stored capacity to do work -- qualitatively distinct from kinetic energy: an object can possess potential energy while at rest (zero kinetic energy), and vice versa.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-WORK: energy = capacity for doing work
SRC-HP-KE: kinetic energy = energy of motion
SRC-PSU-WORKENERGY: potential energy as stored capacity due to position
learningPoints.depthJustification: Energy's general meaning and the kinetic/potential distinction are combined into one qualitative comparison point, analogous to the mass/weight comparison (MM-LP-01) -- both are purely conceptual with no formula bound here. The gravitational potential energy FORMULA (PE=mgh) is deliberately a separate learning point (MM-LP-15), since it is a specific, calculable case, while KE has no formula bound at all here, per the Product Architect's explicit exclusion of KE=(1/2)mv^2 from this batch's mastery content. No cross-domain arithmetic prerequisite is attached, since this learning point has no calculation outcome of its own.
explicitExclusions: KE = (1/2)mv^2 (explicitly excluded as Unit 202 mastery content -- kinetic energy remains a required qualitative concept only)
Elastic/chemical/other specific energy forms beyond kinetic and potential
Conservation of mechanical energy as a formal calculation
applicationTypes: Explain whether a stretched spring, a raised weight, and a moving car each possess kinetic energy, potential energy, or both.

learningPoints.title: Gravitational potential energy and work done against gravity
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain that lifting an object does work against gravity that is stored as gravitational potential energy, and calculate the gravitational potential energy gained using PE=mgh.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Lifting an object does work against the force of gravity; this work is stored as (equals) the gained gravitational potential energy: PE=mgh, where h is the change in vertical height between the start and end positions (not the total distance travelled along any sloped or indirect path), m is mass, and g is a consistent gravitational field strength used throughout the calculation.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-PSU-WORKENERGY: work against gravity becomes stored PE; delta-PE=mgh with delta-h defined as vertical displacement
learningPoints.depthJustification: The work-against-gravity concept and the PE=mgh formula are combined into one learning point, since the formula is simply the calculable form of the same equivalence -- separating them would fragment one coherent outcome. Height (h) is bound explicitly as vertical displacement, not path length, per the Product Architect's locked depth boundary; PE gained is directly proportional to h for fixed m and g (hence FM-LP-10). Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the formula-rearrangement prerequisite (FM-LP-16) was removed, since the evidenced worked examples (and this outcome) only ever calculate PE from m, g and h -- no rearrangement to find h or m from the other quantities is evidenced.
explicitExclusions: Non-vertical/inclined-path work calculations beyond using the net vertical rise
Elastic potential energy or other non-gravitational potential-energy forms
applicationTypes: Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained when a 40 kg load is lifted vertically 3 m.
Explain why sliding a load up a ramp to a given height stores the same potential energy as lifting it straight up to that height.

learningPoints.title: Power: concept and P = W/t
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that power is the rate of doing work and use P=W/t to calculate power, work, or time.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Power is the rate of doing work (equivalently, the rate at which energy is transferred): P=W/t, where W is the work done and t is the time taken. Power's SI unit is the watt, equal to one joule per second.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-POWER: power as rate of doing work, watt unit
SRC-PSU-POWER: P=W/t
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definition and formula combined as one concept, consistent with the pattern already used for work (MM-LP-13) and F=mg (MM-LP-02). Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: the formula-rearrangement prerequisite (FM-LP-16) was removed, since the evidenced worked examples only calculate power from work and time; rearranging P=W/t for W or t (as the outcome still allows) is straightforward substitution-level algebra already covered by FM-LP-13, not the more involved rearrangement skill FM-LP-16 represents elsewhere in this inventory (e.g. solving Fe x de = Fr x dr for an unknown arm length).
explicitExclusions: Instantaneous power / calculus-based rate of change
Electrical power (already evidenced separately in Batch 02)
applicationTypes: Calculate the power developed by a motor that does 3000 J of work in 12 seconds.

learningPoints.title: Efficiency: concept and calculation
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state what efficiency means and calculate it as useful output divided by total input, expressed as a ratio or percentage, using either energy/work values or power values (never mixing the two).
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Efficiency is the proportion of useful work or power delivered by a system's output, compared with the work or power supplied to it as input, expressed as a ratio or percentage: efficiency = W_out/W_in (useful work output over work input), OR, separately, efficiency = P_out/P_in (useful power output over power input) -- these are the two legitimate, dimensionally-compatible forms; a work/energy quantity must never be divided by a power quantity or vice versa. Efficiency can never legitimately exceed 100%, since that would violate conservation of energy.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-PSU-EFFICIENCY: efficiency definition and eta=W_out/W_in=P_out/P_in
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definition and calculation combined, consistent with the pattern used throughout this batch. FM-LP-06/FM-LP-07 (percentage of a quantity; expressing one quantity as a percentage of another) are genuine prerequisites here, since expressing useful output as a percentage of input is exactly what those foundational-mathematics learning points evidence. The work-ratio and power-ratio forms are kept explicitly separate in the outcome and procedure, per the Product Architect's instruction never to mix an energy numerator with a power denominator.
explicitExclusions: Combining an energy/work numerator with a power denominator (or vice versa) -- explicitly excluded as an invalid calculation
Detailed loss-mechanism breakdowns (friction coefficients etc.)
applicationTypes: Calculate the efficiency, as a percentage, of a motor that delivers 450 J of useful work for 600 J of energy input.
Calculate the efficiency of a machine given its useful power output and power input.

learningPoints.title: Legitimate multistep mechanical calculations
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to solve a multistep mechanical problem by correctly chaining together individually-simple relationships from this domain in sequence -- for example, finding the work done lifting an object against gravity from its weight force and height, then using that work to calculate the power required over a given time -- rather than relying on a single formula.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A legitimate multistep mechanical calculation chains several already-evidenced simple relationships from this domain in sequence to reach a result that no single formula gives directly. For example: (1) find the work done raising an object against gravity from its weight force and the vertical height risen (work = weight force x height, the same relationship as gravitational-lifting-work-against-gravity/PE=mgh), then (2) divide that work by the time taken to find the power required (P=W/t). Each step reuses an already-evidenced relationship from this batch (weight/lifting work, lever/gear/pulley relationships, work, power, efficiency) rather than introducing any new formula.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-PSU-POWER (worked-solution PDF, 'Problem 2'): weight force x height = work done lifting a car; work / time = power required -- chaining the gravitational-work and power relationships already evidenced elsewhere in this batch
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept as its own learning point, separate from each individual formula-recognition point, because genuinely multistep problem-solving (chaining two or more relationships, using an intermediate result) is a distinct, more demanding performance level than recognising or applying any one formula alone. Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: this learning point's sole procedure evidence was previously a hydraulic worked example, rejected because hydraulics is explicitly excluded from this batch's mastery scope and an out-of-scope example cannot be the sole procedure evidence for an in-scope learning point merely by calling it an analogy. The replacement worked example (from the already-registered SRC-PSU-POWER source) genuinely chains two in-scope relationships already evidenced elsewhere in this batch -- gravitational lifting work and P=W/t -- even though its own units are imperial (lbs, ft, hp) rather than SI; the chaining PROCEDURE evidenced is unit-system-independent. The formula-rearrangement prerequisite (FM-LP-16) has also been removed, since the replacement example only performs forward substitution at each step, not rearrangement.
explicitExclusions: Hydraulic systems as taught Unit 202 content (the previously-cited hydraulic example is retained only in ACQUISITION-LOG.json and SOURCE-REGISTER.json as a rejected candidate for this specific requirement)
Any single-formula calculation already covered by one of this learning point's own prerequisite learning points
applicationTypes: Given the weight of a component and the height it must be lifted in a stated time, calculate the work done and then the power required.
Given a lever or pulley system lifting a load a stated height in a stated time, calculate the effort force, the work done, and the power developed.

crossDomainPrerequisiteCorrectionNote: Corrected in a Product Architect narrow-correction pass: MM-LP-09 (pulley mechanical advantage by counting rope sections) and MM-LP-10 (now purely conceptual after the power-relationship correction) had their cross-domain arithmetic prerequisites (FM-LP-04, FM-LP-08, FM-LP-13, FM-LP-16) removed entirely, since neither outcome genuinely requires decimal arithmetic, substitution, ratio notation, or formula rearrangement. FM-LP-16 (formula rearrangement) was also removed from MM-LP-13, MM-LP-15, MM-LP-16, and MM-LP-18, since none of their evidenced worked examples demonstrate rearranging the relevant formula for a different unknown -- only forward substitution is evidenced. FM-LP-16 is retained on MM-LP-02, MM-LP-05, and MM-LP-07, whose outcomes and evidence genuinely include finding a different unknown by rearrangement (e.g. m=w/g; solving Fe x de = Fr x dr for an unknown arm or force; solving the gear-ratio relationship for an unknown tooth count or speed).
